facts.original: Dogs have a sense of smell that's 40 times stronger than humans.
facts.text: Dogs have a much more sensitive sense of smell than people; there is no single multiplier that describes every scent or every dog.

facts.original: Dogs can understand about 165 words and gestures.
facts.text: Dogs can learn spoken cues and object names, but vocabulary varies widely with the individual and their training.

facts.original: Dogs are as smart as a two-year-old child.
facts.text: Dogs have different strengths in learning and problem solving. Comparing every dog to a particular human age or assigning one universal intelligence ranking is misleading.

facts.original: A dog’s sense of hearing is more acute than humans.
facts.text: A dog’s sense of hearing is more acute than humans.

facts.original: Dogs have about 1,700 taste buds, compared to humans' 9,000.
facts.text: Dogs have fewer taste buds than people and rely heavily on smell when investigating food.

facts.original: Dogs' noses are wet to absorb scent chemicals.
facts.text: Moisture helps a dog collect scent particles. A wet or dry nose by itself is not a reliable health test.

facts.original: Dogs can be trained to detect diseases like cancer and diabetes.
facts.text: Specially trained dogs have been studied for detecting disease-related odors. They do not replace medical screening or a clinical diagnosis.

facts.original: A dog’s nose print is unique, much like a human fingerprint.
facts.text: A dog’s nose print is unique, much like a human fingerprint.

facts.original: Dogs sweat through their paw pads, not their fur.
facts.text: Dogs have sweat glands in their paw pads, but panting is their main way to release body heat.

facts.original: Many dogs have the instinct to dig and bury objects.
facts.text: Many dogs have the instinct to dig and bury objects.

facts.original: Newfoundlands are excellent swimmers and have webbed feet.
facts.text: Newfoundlands are excellent swimmers and have webbed feet.

facts.original: Basenjis are the only breed that cannot bark.
facts.text: Basenjis are known for an unusual yodel-like vocalization rather than a typical repeated bark; they are not silent.

facts.original: Greyhounds are the fastest dogs, capable of running up to 45 mph.
facts.text: Greyhounds are exceptionally fast sprinters, although an individual dog’s speed depends on fitness, conditions, and measurement.

facts.original: Dogs have three eyelids, including one to keep their eyes moist.
facts.text: Dogs have three eyelids, including one to keep their eyes moist.

facts.original: Bloodhounds can track scents that are over 300 hours old.
facts.text: Scent hounds can follow odor trails, but how far or how long a scent remains detectable depends on the environment, training, and individual dog.

facts.original: The Chihuahua is the smallest breed, while the Mastiff is the largest.
facts.text: Chihuahuas are among the smallest dogs, while Mastiffs are among the heaviest. Height and weight are different measures of size.

facts.original: Dogs can see some colors but are partially colorblind.
facts.text: Dogs see colors, especially blues and yellows, but distinguish reds and greens differently from people.

facts.original: Dogs communicate with each other through body language.
facts.text: Dogs communicate with each other through body language.

facts.original: Dogs have a natural instinct to herd, especially breeds like Border Collies.
facts.text: Dogs have a natural instinct to herd, especially breeds like Border Collies.

facts.original: A dog's heart beats 60–120 times per minute, depending on the breed.
facts.text: A dog’s resting heart rate varies with size, age, excitement, and health; one range does not describe every dog.

facts.original: The Labrador Retriever is one of the most popular breeds worldwide.
facts.text: Labrador Retrievers are well-known sporting dogs with a long history of retrieving work.

facts.original: Dogs often dream, just like humans, and may twitch or bark in their sleep.
facts.text: Dogs experience REM sleep. Twitching or quiet vocalizing during sleep can occur; not every movement tells us what a dog is dreaming about.

facts.original: A dog’s mouth exerts 320 psi of pressure.
facts.text: Bite force varies with the dog and how it is measured. A single pressure value does not describe every dog’s bite.

facts.original: Dogs have existed for over 30,000 years as companions to humans.
facts.text: Dogs were domesticated thousands of years ago. Researchers continue to study exactly when and where that process began.

facts.original: A dog's sense of time lets them anticipate daily routines.
facts.text: A dog's sense of time lets them anticipate daily routines.

facts.original: Dogs can become depressed or anxious if left alone for long periods.
facts.text: Some dogs experience distress when separated from their people. Separation-related behavior deserves patient support and, when needed, professional assessment.

facts.original: Boxers are known for their playful and energetic nature.
facts.text: Boxers are known for their playful and energetic nature.

facts.original: Pugs are one of the most affectionate and charming dog breeds.
facts.text: Pugs are one of the most affectionate and charming dog breeds.

facts.original: Dogs are naturally protective and can be trained to guard their owners.
facts.text: Protective behavior varies between individuals. Teach calm responses and use qualified, reward-based help rather than encouraging aggression.

facts.original: The Dalmatian's distinctive black spots are inherited genetically.
facts.text: The Dalmatian's distinctive black spots are inherited genetically.

facts.original: Golden Retrievers are one of the most popular therapy dog breeds.
facts.text: Some Golden Retrievers work as therapy dogs. Suitability depends on the individual dog’s health, temperament, and training.

facts.original: A dog’s body temperature is typically between 101°F and 102.5°F (about 38°C).
facts.text: A typical normal body temperature for dogs is about 101–102.5°F (38.3–39.2°C).

facts.original: Some dogs, like the Basenji, are known for not barking at all.
facts.text: Basenjis are known for an unusual yodel-like vocalization rather than a typical repeated bark; they are not silent.

facts.original: The Border Collie is often considered the most intelligent dog breed.
facts.text: Dogs have different strengths in learning and problem solving. Comparing every dog to a particular human age or assigning one universal intelligence ranking is misleading.

facts.original: Dogs have been known to aid in search-and-rescue missions.
facts.text: Dogs have been known to aid in search-and-rescue missions.

facts.original: Dogs have an excellent memory and can remember specific events for years.
facts.text: Dogs can retain learned associations and skills. Memory performance depends on the task, experience, age, and individual.

facts.original: Small breeds, such as Chihuahuas, often live longer than large breeds like Great Danes.
facts.text: Lifespan varies considerably. Smaller dogs tend to live longer than giant breeds, but breed and individual health also matter.

facts.original: The Samoyed is known for its "Sammy smile" and fluffy white coat.

facts.original: Saint Bernards were originally bred to rescue people in the Swiss Alps.
facts.text: Saint Bernards have a history of assisting alpine rescue work around the Great St. Bernard Hospice.

facts.original: Some dogs are known to have a "reverse sneezing" reflex, especially small breeds.
facts.text: Reverse sneezing is a series of rapid inward snorts. New, frequent, or distressing episodes should be assessed by a veterinarian.

facts.original: Shiba Inus are an ancient Japanese breed known for their fox-like appearance.

facts.original: Dogs' whiskers are highly sensitive and help them navigate in the dark.
facts.text: Whiskers are sensitive touch hairs that help dogs detect nearby objects and movement.

facts.original: Most dogs have 42 teeth, although this can vary slightly depending on the breed.
facts.text: A complete set of permanent adult dog teeth normally contains 42 teeth; missing or abnormal teeth can occur.

facts.original: The Alaskan Malamute was originally bred for sledding in harsh Arctic conditions.
facts.text: The Alaskan Malamute was originally bred for sledding in harsh Arctic conditions.

facts.original: All dogs have the ability to swim, but some breeds are naturally better swimmers than others.
facts.text: Not every dog can swim safely. Introduce water gradually, supervise closely, and use a properly fitted canine life jacket when appropriate.

facts.original: French Bulldogs are one of the most popular small dog breeds worldwide.
facts.text: French Bulldogs are compact companion dogs with short muzzles; take particular care with heat and strenuous activity.

facts.original: The Beagle is one of the most popular dog breeds in the United States.
facts.text: Beagles are compact scent hounds developed to work in packs.

facts.original: Some dogs, like the Irish Wolfhound, are bred to hunt large game like deer or boar.

facts.original: Dogs' paws have sweat glands, which help them regulate their body temperature.

facts.original: The Dalmatian is born completely white and develops its distinctive spots as it grows older.
facts.text: Dalmatian puppies are usually born with white coats and develop their spots later; some are born with larger colored patches.

facts.original: Chow Chows are known for their lion-like mane and blue-black tongues.

facts.original: Dogs are descendants of wolves, and despite thousands of years of domestication, they still share many behaviors with their wild ancestors.
facts.text: Domestic dogs and modern wolves share ancestry. Domestication has also produced important differences in behavior and development.

facts.original: Dogs’ paws have a unique, individual print, similar to human fingerprints.
facts.text: Paw pads help cushion a dog’s steps and provide traction. Paw prints should not be presented as a proven identification system like human fingerprints.

facts.original: Dogs have been shown to help reduce stress in humans and can even lower blood pressure.

facts.original: The average dog can understand more than 150 words, including commands and names of people or objects.

facts.original: Dogs can detect changes in human emotions and may adjust their behavior accordingly.

facts.original: Dogs are more likely to wag their tail when they are happy, but they also wag it when anxious or frightened.

facts.original: Dogs have been trained to detect bombs, drugs, and even signs of seizures in humans.

facts.original: Some dogs are naturally more independent, like the Basenji, which is known for being aloof and quiet.

goodFoods.name: Chicken (cooked, no bones)
goodFoods.note: Serve plain, fully cooked, skinless chicken; remove every bone.

goodFoods.name: Carrots
goodFoods.note: Wash and cut into small pieces to reduce choking.

goodFoods.name: Blueberries
goodFoods.note: Offer a few washed berries as an occasional treat.

goodFoods.name: Peanut butter (unsweetened and unsalted)
goodFoods.note: Check for xylitol (birch sugar); use only xylitol-free, plain peanut butter sparingly.

goodFoods.name: Sweet potatoes (cooked)
goodFoods.note: Cook until soft; offer plain pieces without seasonings.

goodFoods.name: Pumpkin (puree)
goodFoods.note: Choose plain pumpkin, not sweetened or spiced pie filling.

goodFoods.name: Green beans
goodFoods.note: Serve plain, chopped beans without added salt or sauces.

goodFoods.name: Salmon (cooked, boneless)
goodFoods.note: Fully cook and remove all bones; no seasoning.

goodFoods.name: Bananas
goodFoods.note: Peel and offer a few small pieces; fruit adds sugar.

goodFoods.name: Apples (without seeds)
goodFoods.note: Remove the core and seeds; cut flesh into small pieces.

goodFoods.name: Rice (plain, cooked)
goodFoods.note: Plain cooked rice is an extra, not a complete diet.

goodFoods.name: Eggs (scrambled or boiled)
goodFoods.note: Cook fully without butter, salt, or other seasoning.

goodFoods.name: Spinach
goodFoods.note: High in oxalates; choose another vegetable for dogs prone to urinary stones.

goodFoods.name: Yogurt (unsweetened, plain)
goodFoods.note: Only plain, xylitol-free yogurt; skip if dairy causes digestive upset.

goodFoods.name: Oatmeal (plain, cooked)
goodFoods.note: Cook in water; avoid sweetened or flavored varieties.

goodFoods.name: Cucumber
goodFoods.note: Wash and cut into manageable pieces.

goodFoods.name: Watermelon (without seeds)
goodFoods.note: Remove seeds and rind; offer small pieces of flesh.

goodFoods.name: Turkey (cooked, no bones)
goodFoods.note: Remove skin and bones; cook fully without seasoning.

goodFoods.name: Zucchini
goodFoods.note: Serve plain, washed, and cut into small pieces.

goodFoods.name: Pineapple (fresh, no skin)
goodFoods.note: Remove the tough skin and core; offer a little flesh.

goodFoods.name: Peas (cooked)
goodFoods.note: Plain fresh, frozen, or cooked peas; avoid added salt.

goodFoods.name: Chia seeds
goodFoods.note: Not an essential supplement. Ask before adding seeds to a prescribed diet.

goodFoods.name: Avocado
goodFoods.note: Not a recommended treat; the pit can obstruct and fatty flesh can upset digestion.

goodFoods.name: Almonds
goodFoods.note: Almonds are a poor treat choice because of choking and high-fat concerns.

goodFoods.name: Tomatoes (ripe, no stems or leaves)
goodFoods.note: Only ripe red flesh; keep green tomatoes, stems, and leaves away.

goodFoods.name: Brussels sprouts (cooked)
goodFoods.note: Offer small plain cooked portions; may cause gas.

goodFoods.name: Watercress
goodFoods.note: Do not feed foraged plants; confirm species and suitability with your vet.

goodFoods.name: Broccoli (cooked)
goodFoods.note: Offer only small plain portions; large amounts can irritate digestion.

goodFoods.name: Collard greens (cooked)
goodFoods.note: Ask first for dogs with kidney or bladder stone history.

goodFoods.name: Parsley
goodFoods.note: Type and amount matter; do not use parsley as a supplement without advice.

goodFoods.name: Cherries
goodFoods.note: Cherry flesh is not the main hazard, but pits and plant parts make other fruits a better choice.

goodFoods.name: Cantaloupe
goodFoods.note: Remove seeds and rind; cut flesh into small pieces.

goodFoods.name: Figs
goodFoods.note: Avoid dried or sweetened fruit; ask about fresh fig portions first.

goodFoods.name: Melon
goodFoods.note: Identify the melon; offer only edible flesh without rind or seeds.

goodFoods.name: Squash
goodFoods.note: Serve plain cooked flesh; remove tough skin and seeds.

goodFoods.name: Celery
goodFoods.note: Chop into small pieces; long stalks can be difficult to chew.

goodFoods.name: Beef (lean, cooked, no bones)
goodFoods.note: Cook fully, choose lean cuts, and remove bones and excess fat.

goodFoods.name: Lamb (cooked, lean)
goodFoods.note: Cook fully; remove bones, excess fat, and seasoning.

goodFoods.name: Honey (in moderation)
goodFoods.note: Sugary and unnecessary; avoid for puppies or dogs with relevant medical conditions.

goodFoods.name: Coconut (unsweetened)
goodFoods.note: Use very small plain portions; fat may cause digestive upset.

goodFoods.name: Ricotta cheese (low fat)
goodFoods.note: Small plain portions only if dairy is tolerated; avoid high-fat products.

goodFoods.name: Hummus (without garlic)
goodFoods.note: Hummus recipes may include garlic, salt, and excess fat. Plain cooked chickpeas are simpler.

goodFoods.name: Beets (cooked)
goodFoods.note: Serve plain and ask first if your dog has a stone-forming history.

goodFoods.name: Bran flakes
goodFoods.note: Check for raisins, chocolate, xylitol, and added sugar; not a needed food.

goodFoods.name: Leafy greens
goodFoods.note: Identify the vegetable; not all greens are suitable for every dog.

goodFoods.name: Apricots (without pit)
goodFoods.note: Discard pit, stem, and leaves; ask about an appropriate portion of flesh.

goodFoods.name: Squash (cooked)
goodFoods.note: Cook plain and remove tough skin and seeds.

goodFoods.name: Tilapia (cooked, boneless)
goodFoods.note: Fully cook, remove every bone, and leave unseasoned.

goodFoods.name: Kale (cooked)
goodFoods.note: Contains oxalates and other irritants; safer vegetables are available.

goodFoods.name: Whole wheat pasta (cooked)
goodFoods.note: Plain cooked pasta only, in small portions; avoid sauces and seasonings.

goodFoods.name: Shrimp (cooked, no shells)
goodFoods.note: Cook fully; remove shell, head, and tail; no butter or seasoning.

goodFoods.name: Cod (cooked, boneless)
goodFoods.note: Cook fully and carefully remove bones; no sauces.

goodFoods.name: Asparagus (cooked)
goodFoods.note: Plain cooked pieces are easier to chew; avoid tough stalks and seasonings.

goodFoods.name: Papaya (peeled, without seeds)
goodFoods.note: Remove peel and seeds; offer a little plain ripe flesh.

goodFoods.name: Turnip greens (cooked)
goodFoods.note: Ask about greens and portion size, especially with a prescribed diet.

goodFoods.name: Chia seeds
goodFoods.note: Not an essential supplement. Ask before adding seeds to a prescribed diet.

goodFoods.name: Brussels sprouts (cooked)
goodFoods.note: Offer small plain cooked portions; may cause gas.

goodFoods.name: Arugula
goodFoods.note: Ask about suitability and portions; salad dressings are not appropriate.

badFoods.name: Chocolate
badFoods.note: Keep away; risk depends on cocoa content, amount, and dog size.

badFoods.name: Onions
badFoods.note: Allium vegetables can damage red blood cells, including cooked forms.

badFoods.name: Garlic
badFoods.note: Garlic and garlic powder can damage red blood cells.

badFoods.name: Grapes
badFoods.note: Can cause serious kidney injury; contact a veterinarian after ingestion.

badFoods.name: Raisins
badFoods.note: Dried grapes can cause kidney injury; seek veterinary advice promptly.

badFoods.name: Xylitol (artificial sweetener)
badFoods.note: Also called birch sugar; can cause low blood sugar and liver injury.

badFoods.name: Alcohol
badFoods.note: Alcohol-containing drinks and foods can poison dogs.

badFoods.name: Caffeine
badFoods.note: Keep coffee, tea concentrates, energy drinks, and caffeine products away.

badFoods.name: Macadamia nuts
badFoods.note: Can cause weakness, tremors, and other illness.

badFoods.name: Avocado (in large amounts)
badFoods.note: The pit can obstruct; fatty flesh is not a recommended treat.

badFoods.name: Cherries (with pits)
badFoods.note: Pits can obstruct; chewed pits and other plant parts add toxicity concerns.

badFoods.name: Cooked bones
badFoods.note: Bones can splinter or obstruct the digestive tract.

badFoods.name: Raw dough
badFoods.note: Raw yeast dough can expand and produce alcohol inside the stomach.

badFoods.name: Salt (excessive amounts)
badFoods.note: Excess salt can cause poisoning; keep salty snacks out of reach.

badFoods.name: Raw fish (containing parasites)
badFoods.note: Raw fish can carry pathogens or parasites; use fully cooked boneless fish.

badFoods.name: Apple seeds
badFoods.note: Remove seeds and core before offering apple flesh.

badFoods.name: Peach pits
badFoods.note: Keep pits away; swallowed pits may obstruct and chewed kernels pose added risk.

badFoods.name: Plums (with pits)
badFoods.note: Keep the pit and plant parts away; do not offer whole plums.

badFoods.name: Mustard seeds
badFoods.note: Do not offer mustard seeds or mustard condiments; choose plain foods.

badFoods.name: Hops (used in beer brewing)
badFoods.note: Brewing hops can cause dangerous overheating; seek veterinary care immediately.

badFoods.name: Alcohol-based vanilla extract
badFoods.note: Keep concentrated alcohol-based flavoring extracts out of reach.

badFoods.name: Macadamia nuts
badFoods.note: Can cause weakness, tremors, and other illness.

badFoods.name: Pitted fruits (peaches, plums)
badFoods.note: Remove and discard pits; never offer whole stone fruits.

badFoods.name: Artificial sweeteners (especially xylitol)
badFoods.note: Xylitol is toxic; other sweeteners are not automatically equally toxic. Check ingredients.

badFoods.name: Processed sugars
badFoods.note: Added sugar is unnecessary; excess treats add calories. Not inherently a poison.

badFoods.name: Raw potatoes
badFoods.note: Avoid raw or green potatoes; plain cooked potato flesh is different.

badFoods.name: Tomato leaves and stems
badFoods.note: Green tomato plant parts contain compounds that can cause illness.

badFoods.original: Raw eggs (due to risk of Salmonella)
badFoods.name: Raw eggs (due to risk of Salmonella)
badFoods.note: Raw eggs can carry harmful bacteria; offer fully cooked egg instead.

badFoods.name: Fatty foods (like bacon, hot dogs)
badFoods.note: Fatty, salty meats are poor treats and can trigger digestive problems.

badFoods.name: Chewing gum with xylitol
badFoods.note: Gum containing xylitol is dangerous; seek veterinary advice after ingestion.

badFoods.name: Nutmeg
badFoods.note: Large amounts can cause poisoning; do not offer nutmeg as a treat.

badFoods.name: Rhubarb leaves
badFoods.note: Rhubarb leaves are a toxic plant exposure; keep away.

badFoods.name: Uncooked pork
badFoods.note: Raw pork can carry pathogens; use fully cooked, plain, lean meat.

badFoods.name: Unripe tomatoes
badFoods.note: Avoid green unripe tomatoes; ripe red flesh is a different preparation.

badFoods.name: Foods with too much dairy
badFoods.note: Many dogs poorly tolerate lactose; amount and product matter.

badFoods.name: Cooked chicken bones
badFoods.note: Cooked poultry bones can splinter; remove all bones.

badFoods.name: Pitted fruit skins
badFoods.note: Fruit skins are not all toxic. Identify the fruit; discard pits and unsuitable parts.

badFoods.name: Raw meat (due to parasites)
badFoods.note: Raw meat can expose dogs and people to pathogens.

badFoods.name: Chili peppers
badFoods.note: Spicy peppers can irritate digestion; do not intentionally feed.

badFoods.name: Hemp products
badFoods.note: THC-containing products can poison dogs; hemp foods and CBD products are not interchangeable.

badFoods.name: Pickles
badFoods.note: Often salty and may contain garlic or onions; use plain cucumber instead.

badFoods.name: Fatty meats (gravy, sausage)
badFoods.note: Gravy and sausage may be fatty, salty, or contain alliums.

badFoods.name: Raw sprouts
badFoods.note: Raw sprouts can carry bacteria; do not use as a routine treat.

badFoods.name: Sugar-free candy
badFoods.note: Check the label: xylitol is toxic; sugar-free does not identify every ingredient.

badFoods.name: Tomato paste (contains salt)
badFoods.note: Plain tomato paste is not automatically toxic; avoid added alliums, salt, and seasonings.

badFoods.name: Corn on the cob
badFoods.note: The cob can obstruct; do not let a dog chew or swallow it.

badFoods.name: Milk chocolate
badFoods.note: Contains chocolate compounds harmful to dogs; seek advice after ingestion.

badFoods.name: Blue cheese
badFoods.note: Mold-ripened cheeses can pose risks; use safer treats.

badFoods.name: Sweetened cereals
badFoods.note: Not a useful staple; check for chocolate, raisins, and xylitol.

badFoods.name: Spicy foods
badFoods.note: Spices and sauces may irritate digestion or contain harmful ingredients.

badFoods.name: Sour cream
badFoods.note: Fat and lactose may upset digestion; not a recommended routine treat.

badFoods.name: High-sodium snacks
badFoods.note: Excess salt can be harmful; choose low-salt dog-appropriate treats.

badFoods.name: Frozen foods
badFoods.note: Frozen is not inherently unsafe. Ingredients, choking risk, and storage determine safety.

badFoods.name: Fake cheese products
badFoods.note: Processed cheese products may be salty and fatty; check ingredients.

badFoods.name: Alcoholic beverages
badFoods.note: Alcohol-containing drinks and foods can poison dogs.

badFoods.name: High-fat dairy
badFoods.note: Fat and lactose can cause digestive upset; avoid rich portions.

badFoods.name: Gum containing xylitol
badFoods.note: Gum containing xylitol is dangerous; seek veterinary advice after ingestion.

badFoods.name: Salami
badFoods.note: A salty, fatty processed meat; may also contain garlic or other seasonings.

badFoods.name: Fruit pits (like apricot or nectarine)
badFoods.note: Keep pits away; obstruction and chewed-kernel risks depend on the fruit.

badFoods.name: Uncooked hot dogs
badFoods.note: Poor routine treats because of salt, fat, and choking risk, even when cooked.

badFoods.name: Cooked potatoes and skins
badFoods.note: Plain fully cooked potato is not automatically unsafe because it has skin; avoid green parts.

badFoods.name: Sour milk
badFoods.note: Spoiled dairy can cause illness; discard it.
